Testimony in Support of LD 512: "An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in Secondary Schools with
200 or Fewer Students"
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and the distinguished members of the Committee On Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of LD 512, An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in Secondary Schools with 200 or Fewer Students.
Maine's education system must prioritize the needs of students and their families by ensuring access to the best educational opportunities available. Unfortunately, students residing in smaller school administrative units (SAUs) with limited resources often face restricted academic and extracurricular options. LD 512 offers these students greater flexibility by allowing them to enroll in another SAU's secondary school if accepted, ensuring that all Maine students have access to an education that best fits their needs.
For students in smaller secondary schools, limited course offerings, extracurricular activities, and specialized academic programs can hinder their educational experience. LD 512 empowers families to make the best decision for their child's future by enabling students to enroll in larger, better-resourced schools. This policy ensures that students in rural and smaller districts are not disadvantaged simply because of where they live.
This bill is also a practical and fiscally responsible approach to expanding school choice. Under LD 512, the financial burden of tuition remains within the public school system, as the receiving SAU invoices the resident SAU for payment at the state's maximum allowable tuition rate. This ensures that no undue financial strain is placed on receiving or sending districts while allowing students greater flexibility in their education.
Similar policies have been successfully implemented in other states, providing students in rural areas with access to enhanced learning opportunities while maintaining financial accountability within the public school system.1 Critics may argue that this policy could lead to declines in enrollment for smaller secondary schools. However, students should not be forced to remain in a school that does not adequately meet their needs. Instead of viewing this policy as a threat, smaller schools should see it as an opportunity to innovate, improve their offerings, and better serve their student populations.
1 https://www.ecs.org/50-state-comparison-open-enrollment-policies/

By passing LD 512, Maine will reaffirm its commitment to educational freedom, equity, and opportunity for all students, regardless of geographic constraints. This legislation is a common sense step toward ensuring every student has access to the resources and learning environment necessary to thrive. We urge the committee to support this bill and advance it to the entire Legislature for consideration. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and other members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee,
My name is Jesse Hargrove, I am a high school social studies teacher on leave serving as President of
the Maine Education Association representing 24,000 members ranging from pre-k through higher
education. I write in opposition to LD 512 An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in
Secondary Schools with 200 or Fewer Students. This act will destabilize many of our rural and remote
school districts, and favor families with means, and further drain resources from local communities.
Our mission should be to ensure that ALL students in all schools are provided with opportunities to meet
personal development, transitional, educational, and career goals. While population shifts in our communities are normal, this would inject additional complications that would impact approximately
20% of Maine's public high schools, leaving them vulnerable to erratic student population shifts. It
would make staffing and budgeting decisions for administrators and school committees even more challenging, furthermore the bill lacks provisions for students who decide to return to their local community school after the staffing and budget decisions have been made.
This bill disproportionately advantages families whose personal and professional lives provides for the
flexibility to transport. Without a provision for transportation, only parents who have the time and the
means to bring their students to and from school, in addition to any extracurricular activities. Meanwhile, students from families without that flexibility will remain in a diminished school.
Our schools also serve as community centers for our smaller towns that lack other facilities. Schools bring people together for musical and theatrical performances, athletic events, and a variety of
community functions. When towns people invest in their schools, they invest in their community. I--Iowever, this bill would threaten that vested interest. Parents who have access to outside schools and community resources would have an individual interest to vote down school and municipal budgets to
reduce local property taxes, depriving all of the community benefit.
This bill is also unnecessary. High schools already across the state are already making a variety of local partnerships and arrangements to expand opportunities for all students, including collaboration for athletics, or exchanges with neighboring districts to broaden course offerings for both districts. These partnerships maintain investments and connection in our communities, while expanding student opportunities. Students can also pursue opportunities through a variety of Career and Technical Education offerings as well as Early College programs offered through Maine's Universities and

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Education and
Cultural Affairs Committee:
LD 512, An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in Secondary Schools with
200 or Fewer Students would provide rural students with school choice at the secondary level if their residential school administrative unit (SAU) has total resident student count of 200 or fewer. Title 20-A provides the opportunity and eligibility provisions for secondary students to attend a school in another unit, including units that have a small resident student count. Existing
statute caps this eligibility at 10 or fewer students. This bill would establish a new section of
statute to provide this opportunity in cases where there are 200 or fewer students.
The Maine DOE has heard how important place-based learning is, and these rural communities
frequently report that these schools are vital to the students and the learning they receive there, for community identity, and for social cohesion.
The Maine DOE has identified 53 schools that each enroll fewer than 200 students. While LD
512 assumes that this will only affect secondary enrollment, Maine schools are not as easily
categorized. Of the 53 schools that the Maine DOE has identified, 17 of them are exclusively 9-
12 secondary schools. The remainder are organized in a combination of grades PreK or Kindergarten through 12, grades 7 through 12, and grades 6 through 12. Three of these schools
are charter schools. These schools collectively enroll over 3,500 students.
Maine families with concerns about their chi1dren's best interest at a small school may take advantage of existing student transfer options (also known as superintendents` agreements)
outlined in Title 20-A �5205.

TO: Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
FROM: Easton School Department
RE: In Opposition of LD 512: An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in Secondary Schools with 200 or Fewer Students
Date: March 12, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is Laura Hunter and I am the principal at Easton Jr/Sr High School. I am testifying as a concerned constituent and stakeholder in our local educational system to express my opposition to LD 512 as currently written.
While I appreciate the goal of increasing educational opportunities for students in small secondary schools, I have significant concerns about both the feasibility and the potential unintended consequences of this bill. My primary concerns include:
1. Fiscal Responsibility and Resource Allocation: The proposal, as drafted, may impose an unsustainable financial burden on local communities and the state. Redirecting funds or creating new programs without a robust analysis of long-term costs risks diverting resources from other critical educational initiatives. In particular, schools that already struggle with limited budgets could face additional challenges in meeting new administrative and programmatic requirements.
2. Equity and Implementation Challenges: Small schools serve a diverse range of communities with unique local needs. A one-size-fits-all statewide mandate does not adequately address the differing circumstances among rural, suburban, and economically disadvantaged areas. Rather than expanding opportunities uniformly, the bill may inadvertently widen existing disparities by providing benefits that are easier to implement in some communities than in others.

3. Risk of a Downward Spiral:
The loss of students could trigger a vicious cycle. Fewer students mean reduced funding, forcing us to cut programs, staff, or extracurricular activities. These reductions would make our school less appealing, prompting more students to leave and further eroding our resources. In Aroostook County, where most secondary schools have fewer than 200 students, this bill could destabilize multiple districts, pushing them toward closure and accelerating the decline of rural education.
4. Disruption to Budgeting and Staffing
The bill mandates that parents notify us by April 1st of their intent to transfer and provide an acceptance letter by May 1st. This timeline creates significant uncertainty in enrollment numbers, making it nearly impossible to plan budgets, staffing, or course offerings accurately. We might overstaff in anticipation of retaining students, only to face last-minute cuts--or understaff and scramble to adjust. Such instability undermines our ability to provide a consistent, high-quality education.
5. Devastation to Rural Communities:
Small schools like ours are the lifeblood of rural communities in Aroostook County. We employ residents, host community events, and attract families to the area. If this bill weakens or closes schools by driving students away, it could devastate our local economy, lower property values, and erode the social fabric that binds us together. Families may leave the region entirely, hastening the population decline already challenging rural Maine.
6. Potential for Adverse Selection
The bill does not specify criteria for acceptance by receiving schools, raising the risk that they might selectively enroll high-achieving or low-cost students while rejecting those with greater needs, such as special education students. This adverse selection could leave small schools with a higher proportion of students requiring more resources, further straining our budgets and widening achievement gaps.
7. Local Control and Flexibility: Local education agencies possess the expertise and intimate knowledge of their students' needs. Centralized programs may undermine local control by imposing standardized criteria that do not reflect the particular challenges and strengths of individual school districts. Effective educational reform should empower local leaders to design solutions that are tailored to their community rather than applying a prescriptive model across the state.

I would also like to add that small schools can be and are successful. In Easton we have students going to ivy league schools, placing in competitions against class B schools,and
continue to be a top performing school across the state.

Conclusion LD 512, while well-intentioned, could be catastrophic for small schools in Aroostook County and beyond. It threatens our financial stability, educational quality, and community vitality, all while failing to address the root challenges facing rural education. I urge the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee to reject this bill and instead pursue policies that bolster small schools, ensuring they remain vibrant hubs of learning and community life. Our students, staff, and families deserve no less.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I remain available should you require further details regarding my perspective. Sincerely,
Laura A. Hunter

Good Morning. Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and
members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. I am
Norman Higgins, a former three term State Representative from Dover-Foxcroft. I want to thank Senator Guerin for sponsoring LD 512, An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in
Secondary Schools with 200 or Fewer Students.
In the past two decades we have experienced a dramatic decline in
enrollment at our secondary schools in rural Maine. As a former teacher and high school principal, I have experienced the challenge of providing a comprehensive curriculum in a rural high school.
Today, we know that due to diminished enrollments, resulting in
reduced funding allocations, rural high schools are not able to provide the academic opportunities that are available at larger
schools. It is well documented that in math, science, foreign languages, the arts and advanced level courses that access is limited in rural high schools. The result has a negative impact on student aspirations and access to higher education. Student success at this level, due to lack of opportunities at the high school
level, is challenging.
In 2007 the Maine Legislature passed legislation to promote school administration consolidation and with the intent to reduce the
number of small high schools. I was the Project Manager for four
years on behalf of the Maine Department of Education. I facilitated numerous public meetings attended by hundreds of citizens in rural Maine. The results were a robust rejection especially in rural Maine.
The only high school merger was between Jay and Livermore. In
2017, the Regional Integrated High School Construction initiative

was launched. Four regional proposals were submitted and in December of 2024 the final applicant withdrew their application.
While common sense informs us of the need to provide equitable
academic opportunities for high school students the ability to change the system has not happened.

The process of utilizing the Superintendent Agreement is not an
effective response to the current situation. Its interpretation by school boards and Superintendents varies from school district to
school district. The appeals process is cumbersome and consumes
significant time at the DOE and the State Board of Education. In
addition, the process must be repeated on an annual basis.

This legislation proposes an alternative process to allow students to
transfer to another high school to address their academic needs. The bill is targeted and specific and not intended to address the
issue of school choice. This legislation provides increased
opportunity for students to have equitable access to academic programs regardless of their geographic residence.

l will be at the work session and welcome the opportunity to work
with the Departmentof Education and this committee on this

legislation.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Pierce, and members of the joint standing committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:

My name is Senator Stacey Guerin and I represent Senate District 4 which includes
all of Piscataquis County and ll towns in Penobscot County. I am here today to
introduce LD 512, "An Act to Provide Educational Opportunities for Students in
Secondary Schools with 200 or Fewer Students."
This bill is a crucial step toward ensuring that all students, regardless of where they live, have access to the educational opportunities they deserve. For students in small school districts with fewer than 200 students, educational options can be very limited. These students often lack access to specialized programs, extracurricular
activities, or resources that larger districts can offer. By allowing parents and
students to choose a school outside of their district, this bill gives families the flexibility to seek out the best fit for their child's needs and interests.

enough time to plan for the upcoming year. It also ensures that funding is allocated
appropriately, with the receiving district invoicing the resident district for the per-
pupil rate, not exceeding the state's maximum allowable tuition.
This bill represents a step forward in providing equitable access to education and
extracurricular activities while empowering families to make decisions that are in
the best interest of their children. I believe it will help level the playing field for students in smaller districts by giving them and their families this option.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I urge you to support this important
legislation.

TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO
L.D. 512
AN ACT TO PROVIDE EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES FOR STUDENTS IN SECONDARY SCHOOLS WITH 200 OR FEWER STUDENTS
March 12, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee. I am Steven Bailey, the executive director for Maine School Management Association, testifying
on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School
Superintendents Association in opposition to L.D. 512.
Article VIII of the Maine Constitution states: "Education. Section 1. Legislature shall require towns to support public schools; duty of Legislature.
A general diffusion of the advantages of education being essential to the preservation of the rights and
liberties of the people; to promote this important object, the Legislature are authorized, and it shall be their duty to require, the several towns to make suitable provision, at their own expense, for the
support and maintenance ofpublic schools. "
Additionally, Title 20-A MSRA � 5202 speaks to Residence and where a student is eligible to attend.
"2. General rule. A person is eligible to attend schools in the school administrative unit where the
person's parent resides, where the person resides upon reaching the age of 18 years or upon becoming
an emancipated minor. A federal installation shall be considered part of the school administrative unit in which it is located. "
Families live where they choose to reside. Very often that decision includes where they wish their children to attend school. Schools are the lifeblood of the community and so often are the identity of the community. Given the desire for local control, following the requirement to join together after the 2008-2009 school consolidation bill, there have been at least 33 school district divorces where a smaller district has successfully separated from a forced marriage during the period of consolidation.
This was a desire by the community for local control, to have control over their own expenditures, and to
retain the individual identity where they can express the community pride they wished to display. Local schools are community institutions and serve an important purpose, as a gathering place and center of community life. As of this writing there are 20 public secondary schools with less than 200 students (grades 912). They are the lifeblood of their communities, many that are multiple miles from any other opportunity to
attend a public secondary school.
L.D. 512 is clearly a school choice bill, providing parents of a student within a secondary school with fewer than 200 students to enroll their child within a secondary school of their choice different from their resident school. If this bill were to pass, a resident town would be required to pay tuition to the receiving school

Given the responsibility of the town to provide, at their own expense, for the education of the students that

reside within their municipality, losing just a few students could be the beginning of a death knell for smaller
